title: Advanced Critical Reasoning
tagline: Year 4 — Hidden assumptions, causal flaws, sampling errors, paradoxes, evaluation of evidence and parallel reasoning in short arguments

introduction.overview: Advanced critical reasoning goes beyond naming the conclusion. It asks you to rank evidence, find the weakest link, tell correlation from cause, notice an unrepresentative sample, resolve an apparent contradiction and evaluate what extra information would settle a dispute. Each type is a question about the gap between premises and conclusion, so the first move is always to state that gap in one line.
introduction.placementRelevance: Advanced critical-reasoning items are the discriminating questions in management and campus verbal sections.
introduction.realWorldContext: Judging proposals, studies and claims in reports uses these same questions.

learningObjectives: State the gap in one line
Identify unrepresentative samples and part-whole errors
Choose the most useful evidence to evaluate a claim
Resolve paradoxes with a reconciling fact

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Strengthen: close the gap or rule out alternatives. Weaken: open the gap or supply an alternative. Assumption: negate it and the argument fails.

coreDefinitions: Gap: the unstated link between premise and conclusion.
Alternative explanation: another cause for the same evidence.
Unrepresentative sample: a group that differs from the population.
Composition error: assuming the whole has a property because each part does.
Evaluation: choosing information that would best test the claim.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Every flawed argument skips a step. Naming the skipped step answers the question.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Write "Premise → Conclusion; gap: assumes…". Then test each option against the gap.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Correlation trap
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: A with B ⇏ A causes B

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Sample test
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Is the sample like the population?

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Paradox
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Find a fact true for both observations

mainNarrative: "Everyone promoted this year works late, so working late leads to promotion." The gap: perhaps people who are ambitious both work late and get promoted, or promoted people are given more work. The flaw is mistaking correlation for cause.
"Cities with more police have more crime, so police cause crime." Weaken it by reversing the direction: cities add police when crime is already rising.
"A poll of gym visitors found 85% support a ban on junk-food advertising, so most residents support it." The sample is not representative of the residents.
To evaluate "the reading programme works because scores rose 10%", ask how scores changed in similar schools without the programme.
To resolve a paradox such as lower prices with higher profit, find a fact that makes both true: so many more customers came that the total margin rose.

deepDiveAspects.title: Necessary versus sufficient
deepDiveAspects.content: An assumption need only make the argument possible, not prove it.

deepDiveAspects.title: Composition and division
deepDiveAspects.content: A property of the parts need not hold for the whole, and vice versa.

solvedExamples.title: Reverse cause
solvedExamples.question: Cities with more police have more crime, so more police cause more crime. Which fact weakens this most?

steps.title: Fact
steps.explanation: Cities add police when crime is already rising.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: Cities add police when crime is already rising

solvedExamples.title: Sampling
solvedExamples.question: A poll of gym visitors shows 85% support a junk-food advertising ban. The council concludes most residents support it. What is wrong?
solvedExamples.finalAnswer: The sample is not representative of residents

solvedExamples.title: Evaluate
solvedExamples.question: A school says its reading programme works because scores rose 10%. What information is most useful?

steps.title: Info
steps.explanation: Scores in similar schools without the programme.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: How scores changed in similar schools without the programme

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: State the gap in one line, then choose the option that widens, closes or crosses it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Picking an option that repeats the premise

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Eliminate options that do not touch the gap.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Wrong options are often true but irrelevant.

easy.question:
Argument: Many of our competitors have moved to remote work and reported lower office costs. Our office lease is expensive. We should therefore consider moving to remote work.

Which of the following is the main conclusion of the argument?
options: Many competitors have moved to remote work.
We should consider moving to remote work.
Competitors reported lower office costs.
Our office lease is expensive.
easy.correctAnswer: We should consider moving to remote work.
easy.explanation: The word "therefore" marks the conclusion; the rest are premises.

easy.question:
Argument: The city should install more streetlights, because well-lit streets deter crime.

Which of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
options: The streets targeted by the plan are currently poorly lit.
Streetlights are cheap to run.
Crime is highest at night in every city.
Residents have asked for streetlights.
easy.correctAnswer: The streets targeted by the plan are currently poorly lit.
easy.explanation: If the targeted streets were already well lit, more lights would add nothing, so the plan assumes they are poorly lit.

easy.question:
Argument: A coffee chain says its new loyalty app increases visits, because average weekly visits per member rose after the app launched.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
options: The app was downloaded a million times.
The coffee is cheaper than in other chains.
Members receive a free drink each month.
Weekly visits of non-members stayed unchanged over the same period.
easy.correctAnswer: Weekly visits of non-members stayed unchanged over the same period.
easy.explanation: It rules out a general rise in visits, so the app is more likely the cause.

intermediate.question:
Argument: A restaurant lowered the price of its set meal, yet its profit rose.

Which of the following best resolves the apparent paradox?
options: The lower price attracted so many more customers that total profit increased.
Competitors also lowered their prices.
The set meal is made of cheaper ingredients.
The restaurant has a large dining room.
intermediate.correctAnswer: The lower price attracted so many more customers that total profit increased.
intermediate.explanation: If many more customers came, total profit can rise even with a lower profit per meal.

intermediate.question:
Argument: Students who attended the revision sessions scored higher than those who did not, so the sessions improved scores.

Which of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
options: All students were invited to the sessions.
The sessions were held in the afternoon.
Teachers prepared the sessions carefully.
The students who attended were not already the higher-scoring students.
intermediate.correctAnswer: The students who attended were not already the higher-scoring students.
intermediate.explanation: If better students were the ones who attended, their higher scores would not show the effect of the sessions.

intermediate.question:
Argument: A poll of 200 visitors to a gym found that 85 per cent support a ban on junk-food advertising. The council concludes that most residents support the ban.

The reasoning in the argument is flawed because it
options: uses a sample that is too large
attacks opponents of the ban
assumes a ban is easy to enforce
bases a claim about all residents on a group that is not representative
intermediate.correctAnswer: bases a claim about all residents on a group that is not representative
intermediate.explanation: Gym visitors may be more health-conscious than the average resident.

advanced.question:
Argument: The company's hiring freeze will save money. However, a freeze overloads existing staff and raises turnover, and replacing staff costs more than the salary saved. So the freeze is likely to cost more than it saves.

Which of the following is the main conclusion of the argument?
options: A hiring freeze saves salary.
A freeze overloads existing staff.
The hiring freeze is likely to cost more than it saves.
Replacing staff is costly.
advanced.correctAnswer: The hiring freeze is likely to cost more than it saves.
advanced.explanation: The last sentence, introduced by "So", is the conclusion.

advanced.question:
Argument: Each part of the machine is cheap, so the machine is cheap.

The reasoning in the argument is flawed because it
options: attacks the sellers of the machine
assumes that the whole has a property because each part has it
relies on an expert
uses a sample that is too small
advanced.correctAnswer: assumes that the whole has a property because each part has it
advanced.explanation: The sum of many cheap parts may still be expensive: a composition error.

placementStyle.question:
Argument: Cities with more police officers have more crime, so more police cause more crime.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
options: Police officers are well trained.
Cities add police officers when crime is already rising.
Crime is reported more in cities.
Most crimes are minor.
placementStyle.correctAnswer: Cities add police officers when crime is already rising.
placementStyle.explanation: It reverses the direction of cause: crime leads to more police.

placementStyle.question:
Argument: Hospitals have added beds, yet waiting times for admission have increased.

Which of the following best resolves the apparent paradox?
options: The number of patients seeking admission has grown faster than the number of beds.
Beds are cleaned more often.
Hospitals have more doctors.
The new beds are more comfortable.
placementStyle.correctAnswer: The number of patients seeking admission has grown faster than the number of beds.
placementStyle.explanation: If demand grew faster than supply, waiting times can rise even as beds increase.

placementStyle.question:
Argument: A ban on single-use cups will reduce litter, because people will bring their own cups.

Which of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
options: Cafés will lose customers.
Reusable cups are cheap.
Litter is a serious problem.
Customers will actually bring reusable cups rather than switching to other disposable items.
placementStyle.correctAnswer: Customers will actually bring reusable cups rather than switching to other disposable items.
placementStyle.explanation: If people switch to other disposables, litter would not fall.
